props.title: Still Life

sections.content: Still Life marks a defining moment in Chinese director Jia Zhangke's exploration of rapid modernization's human cost. Set against the backdrop of the Three Gorges Dam project, the film captures the literal drowning of history as entire cities vanish underwater. It shares thematic DNA with other masterful slow cinema works like Goodbye, Dragon Inn (2003) and An Elephant Sitting Still (2018), using long takes and minimal dialogue to convey profound displacement. The film's visual poetry recalls Yellow Earth (1984), but with a sharper political edge.

sections.content: Jia Zhangke's signature blend of documentary and fiction reaches its apex in Still Life. Like his earlier Unknown Pleasures (2002) and later A Touch of Sin (2013), the film captures China's jarring transition from socialism to hypercapitalism. The demolition workers' methodical destruction of homes becomes a haunting metaphor, while surreal touches - like a building suddenly taking off like a rocket - inject magical realism into documentary-style observation.

The film's influence resonates through contemporary Chinese cinema, particularly in works like Kaili Blues (2015) and Long Day's Journey Into Night (2018). These films share Still Life's contemplative pacing and concern with memory and place. The protagonist's search for his wife mirrors broader themes of displacement seen in films like Last Train Home (2009) and Up the Yangtze (2007), both documenting the human impact of China's economic miracle. sections.content: The film's stunning cinematography by Yu Lik-wai transforms industrial demolition into visual poetry. Each frame could be a photograph, recalling the work of artists like Edward Burtynsky. This aesthetic approach influenced later films like Behemoth (2015) and Dead Pigs (2018), which similarly examine China's environmental and social challenges through a sophisticated visual language.
